items.q: Which long mountain range runs along Vietnam's border with Laos?
items.h: The Trường Sơn, also called the Annamite Range, runs for about 1,100 km.

items.q: Fansipan is nicknamed the 'Roof of' which region?
items.h: Fansipan, in the Hoàng Liên Sơn range near Sa Pa, is the highest peak in Indochina.

items.q: Chữ Quốc ngữ, the way Vietnamese is written, uses which alphabet?
items.h: Chữ Quốc ngữ uses Latin letters plus marks that show each word's tone.

items.q: Sơn Đoòng cave is so big that it has its own what inside?
items.h: Where Sơn Đoòng's roof has fallen in, sunlight lets a real jungle grow inside.

items.q: Hội An's famous covered bridge is named after traders from where?
items.h: Hội An's Japanese Covered Bridge was built in the 1590s and is on the 20,000 đồng note.

items.q: Vietnamese 'ma' and 'má' sound different only in their what?
items.h: Vietnamese has six tones, so ma, má, mà, mả, mã and mạ are six different words.

items.q: Which pink blossom decorates homes in northern Vietnam at Tết?
items.h: In the north, families bring home peach blossom for Tết; in the south, yellow mai.

items.q: Which Hà Nội dish is grilled pork with cold rice noodles?
items.h: Bún chả comes with fresh herbs and a sweet, sour dipping sauce called nước chấm.

items.q: What is 'cơm' in Vietnamese?
items.h: Cơm means cooked rice, and 'ăn cơm' (eat rice) can simply mean 'have a meal'.

items.q: Which imaginary line circles Earth halfway between the poles?
items.h: The equator is 0° latitude and splits Earth into northern and southern hemispheres.

items.q: What is the line of 0° longitude called?
items.h: The prime meridian runs from pole to pole through Greenwich in London.

items.q: Each time zone is roughly how many degrees of longitude wide?
items.h: Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so each hour of time matches 15° of longitude.

items.q: Crossing which line in the Pacific changes the date by a day?
items.h: The International Date Line roughly follows 180° longitude through the Pacific.

items.q: Which strait separates Spain from Africa?
items.h: At its narrowest the Strait of Gibraltar is only about 14 km wide.

items.q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
items.h: Gold's symbol Au comes from aurum, the Latin word for gold.

items.q: Which element has the chemical symbol Fe?
items.h: Fe comes from ferrum, the Latin word for iron.

items.q: Who used a prism to show that white light is a mix of colours?
items.h: In the 1660s Newton split sunlight with a prism and named seven rainbow colours.

items.q: What is it called when light bends as it passes into water?
items.h: Refraction makes a straw standing in a glass of water look bent or broken.

items.q: Which part of an atom has a negative charge?
items.h: Electrons whizz around an atom's nucleus, which holds protons and neutrons.

items.q: Which planet has the Great Red Spot, a giant storm?
items.h: Astronomers have watched Jupiter's Great Red Spot for more than 150 years.

items.q: Which planet takes longer to spin once than to go round the Sun?
items.h: Venus takes 243 Earth days to spin once but only 225 to go round the Sun.

items.q: What is the name of the biggest volcano on Mars?
items.h: Olympus Mons on Mars is about two and a half times as tall as Mount Everest.

items.q: Titan, a moon with a thick, hazy sky, circles which planet?
items.h: Titan, Saturn's largest moon, has lakes of liquid methane instead of water.

items.q: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are which kind of planet?
items.h: The four inner planets are rocky; the outer four are giants made of gas and ice.

items.q: Which group of animals do frogs, toads and newts belong to?
items.h: Most amphibians start life in water and later breathe air with lungs.

items.q: What is an animal without a backbone called?
items.h: Most animal species are invertebrates, from worms and snails to octopuses.

items.q: Which of these mammals lays eggs?
items.h: The platypus and the echidnas are the only mammals that lay eggs.

items.q: Which of these mammals can truly fly?
items.h: Sugar gliders and colugos only glide, but bats flap their wings to really fly.

items.q: What are animals that are active at night called?
items.h: Owls, bats and hedgehogs are nocturnal: they rest by day and come out at night.

items.q: Which organ makes bile to help digest fats?
items.h: Bile from the liver is stored in the gall bladder and helps break down fats.

items.q: Which tube carries food from your mouth to your stomach?
items.h: Muscles in the oesophagus squeeze food down, so you can even swallow upside down.

items.q: Which tiny tubes link your arteries to your veins?
items.h: Capillaries are so narrow that red cells pass through them in single file.

items.q: Which part of your eye changes shape to focus?
items.h: Tiny muscles make your eye's lens fatter or thinner to focus on near or far things.

items.q: Photosynthesis makes glucose and which gas?
items.h: The oxygen we breathe comes from plants and algae doing photosynthesis.

items.q: Which type of rock forms when heat and pressure change other rocks?
items.h: Marble is a metamorphic rock, made when limestone is squeezed and heated.

items.q: Which layer of the atmosphere do we live in?
items.h: Nearly all weather happens in the troposphere, the lowest layer of the air.

items.q: What is a living thing that breaks down dead plants called?
items.h: Fungi and bacteria are decomposers: they recycle dead leaves into rich soil.

items.q: Which Venetian traveller wrote about his journey to China?
items.h: Marco Polo reached the court of Kublai Khan in the 1270s and stayed for years.

items.q: Whose expedition was the first to sail all the way round the world?
items.h: Magellan's fleet left Spain in 1519; one ship, led by Elcano, got home in 1522.

items.q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still stands?
items.h: Of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, only the Great Pyramid of Giza survives.

items.q: Which ancient people built Machu Picchu?
items.h: The Inca built Machu Picchu high in Peru's Andes mountains in the 1400s.

items.q: In which country was paper first made?
items.h: Paper was first made in China about 2,000 years ago, from soaked plant fibres.

items.q: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
items.h: Michelangelo spent four years painting the Sistine Chapel ceiling, from 1508 to 1512.

items.q: Which composer wrote the violin concertos 'The Four Seasons'?
items.h: Vivaldi's The Four Seasons has one violin concerto for each season of the year.

items.q: Which of these languages uses the Cyrillic alphabet?
items.h: Cyrillic is used for Russian, Bulgarian, Serbian and other languages.

items.q: Which painter is famous for his pictures of water lilies?
items.h: Claude Monet painted the water lilies in his garden at Giverny again and again.

items.q: What is the next prime number after 7?
items.h: A prime has exactly two factors, 1 and itself; 9 is not prime because 3 × 3 = 9.

items.q: What do the four angles inside a quadrilateral add up to?
items.h: Any four-sided shape can be cut into two triangles: 180° + 180° = 360°.

items.q: What is the area of a rectangle 6 cm long and 4 cm wide?
items.h: Area of a rectangle = length × width, so 6 × 4 = 24 square centimetres.

items.q: How many millilitres are there in a litre?
items.h: Milli means one thousandth, so a millilitre is a thousandth of a litre.

items.q: Vietnam's two great rice deltas are the Mekong and which river's?
items.h: The Red River is named after the reddish-brown silt that colours its water.

items.q: In Vietnamese, what does 'nước' mean?
items.h: Nước means water, and đất nước, 'land and water', means country.

items.q: The đàn bầu's notes slide up and down when the player bends a what?
items.h: The đàn bầu has just one string, bent by a flexible rod to make singing, sliding notes.

items.q: Which world body named Hạ Long Bay a World Heritage Site?
items.h: UNESCO lists Hạ Long Bay, Huế's monuments and Hội An's old town as World Heritage.

items.q: Gỏi cuốn, Vietnam's fresh spring rolls, are wrapped in what?
items.h: Gỏi cuốn wrap prawns, herbs and noodles in thin rice paper, and are not fried.

items.q: Cà phê sữa đá is iced coffee made with which kind of milk?
items.h: Vietnamese coffee drips slowly through a little metal filter called a phin.

items.q: What is the Vietnamese word for 'one'?
items.h: Counting in Vietnamese goes một, hai, ba, bốn, năm: one, two, three, four, five.

items.q: Which country lies along Vietnam's northern border?
items.h: Vietnam borders China to the north, and Laos and Cambodia to the west.

items.q: Where is the deepest part of Earth's oceans?
items.h: The Mariana Trench in the Pacific is deeper than Mount Everest is tall.

items.q: Which is the largest country in the world by area?
items.h: Russia is so wide that it stretches across 11 time zones.

items.q: What is the capital of Canada?
items.h: Ottawa, not the bigger city of Toronto, is Canada's capital.

items.q: Nairobi is the capital of which African country?
items.h: Nairobi has a national park with lions and giraffes right next to the city.

items.q: The Tropic of what lies about 23° south of the equator?
items.h: The Tropic of Cancer is north of the equator; the Tropic of Capricorn is south of it.

items.q: What is the chemical symbol for sodium?
items.h: Na comes from natrium, an old Latin name for sodium.

items.q: What are the columns of the periodic table called?
items.h: Elements in the same group, like lithium and sodium, behave in similar ways.

items.q: Which unit is used to measure electrical resistance?
items.h: The ohm is named after Georg Ohm, a German teacher and scientist.

items.q: In a series circuit, if one bulb breaks, what do the others do?
items.h: A series circuit has only one loop, so one break stops the electricity flowing.

items.q: Which colour of light bends the most in a prism?
items.h: Violet bends most and red least, so a prism spreads white light into a rainbow.

items.q: What is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kg, called?
items.h: Your mass stays the same on the Moon, but you weigh less because gravity is weaker.

items.q: Which is the smallest planet in our solar system?
items.h: Mercury is even smaller than Ganymede, Jupiter's biggest moon.

items.q: Phobos and Deimos are the two moons of which planet?
items.h: Mars's two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, are shaped like lumpy potatoes.

items.q: What does a light year measure?
items.h: A light year is how far light travels in one year: about 9.5 trillion km.

items.q: Which star sits almost directly above Earth's North Pole?
items.h: Polaris, the North Star, hardly moves in the sky, so travellers used it to find north.

items.q: Who was the first woman to travel into space?
items.h: Valentina Tereshkova flew into space in 1963 and went round Earth 48 times.

items.q: What is a shark's skeleton made of?
items.h: Shark skeletons are cartilage, the same bendy stuff that shapes your nose and ears.

items.q: Which whale has a long spiral tusk?
items.h: A narwhal's tusk is really a very long tooth that grows out through its lip.

items.q: Which bird lays the biggest eggs?
items.h: One ostrich egg is about as heavy as two dozen hen's eggs.

items.q: What do we call one kind of living thing, such as the lion?
items.h: Scientists have named well over a million species of animals so far.

items.q: Which sea creature has no brain, no heart and no bones?
items.h: Jellyfish have drifted through the oceans for over 500 million years.

items.q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
items.h: Your heart has two atria at the top and two ventricles at the bottom.

items.q: Which part of the eye turns light into signals for the brain?
items.h: The retina at the back of your eye has millions of cells called rods and cones.

items.q: What are the tiny air sacs in your lungs called?
items.h: Your lungs hold hundreds of millions of alveoli, where oxygen passes into your body.

items.q: What joins your muscles to your bones?
items.h: Tendons join muscles to bones; ligaments join bones to other bones at joints.

items.q: What is molten rock called while it is still underground?
items.h: Molten rock is called magma underground and lava once it pours out of a volcano.

items.q: Earth's crust is broken into giant pieces called what?
items.h: Tectonic plates move a few centimetres a year, about as fast as fingernails grow.

items.q: Which gas makes up most of the air we breathe?
items.h: Air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, with a little argon and carbon dioxide.

items.q: What is a community of living things and their surroundings?
items.h: A pond is an ecosystem: plants, animals, water, soil and sunlight working together.

items.q: Who sailed west from Spain in 1492 and reached the Americas?
items.h: Columbus was trying to reach Asia by sailing west when he arrived in the Caribbean.

items.q: Who first sailed from Europe to India round the tip of Africa?
items.h: Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498 after sailing round the Cape of Good Hope.

items.q: The Parthenon stands on which rocky hill in Athens?
items.h: The Parthenon was built on the Acropolis nearly 2,500 years ago, from white marble.

items.q: Which ancient people wrote in cuneiform on clay tablets?
items.h: Cuneiform, from ancient Mesopotamia, is one of the oldest known kinds of writing.

items.q: Which Spanish artist helped invent Cubism?
items.h: Picasso and Georges Braque invented Cubism, showing things from many sides at once.

items.q: Which Austrian composer wrote the opera 'The Magic Flute'?
items.h: Mozart wrote his first little pieces at five and over 600 works in his life.

items.q: The word 'alphabet' comes from which two Greek letters?
items.h: Alpha and beta are the first two letters of the Greek alphabet.

items.q: Which Japanese writing uses characters borrowed from Chinese?
items.h: Japanese mixes kanji with two sound alphabets, hiragana and katakana.

items.q: Which partner dance began in Buenos Aires and Montevideo?
items.h: The tango grew up by the River Plate in Argentina and Uruguay in the late 1800s.

items.q: What is the square root of 169?
items.h: 13 × 13 = 169, so 13 is the square root of 169.

items.q: How many faces does a triangular prism have?
items.h: A triangular prism has 2 triangles and 3 rectangles: 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices.

items.q: What is 15% of 200?
What is the distance all the way round a circle called?
items.h: A circle's circumference is just over 3 times its diameter: that number is pi.

items.q: Hạ Long Bay's name means 'where the dragon' does what?
items.h: Legend says a dragon came down and spat out jewels that became Hạ Long's islands.

items.q: Huế's Imperial City holds a Forbidden City named after which colour?
items.h: The Nguyễn emperors and their families lived in Huế's Purple Forbidden City.

items.q: In a water puppet show, where do the puppeteers stand?
items.h: Puppeteers stand waist-deep in water behind a bamboo screen, working long poles.

items.q: What is phở bò made with?
items.h: Bò means beef and gà means chicken, so phở bò is beef phở and phở gà is chicken.

items.q: Tết, the Lunar New Year, falls in late January or which month?
items.h: Tết follows the Moon, so its date moves each year, between late January and February.

items.q: Vietnamese 'sơn mài' pictures are made with which shiny coating?
items.h: Sơn mài artists paint layer after layer of lacquer, then polish it until it shines.

items.q: Which city's Dragon Bridge breathes fire over the Hàn River?
items.h: On weekend nights, Đà Nẵng's Dragon Bridge breathes real fire and sprays water.

items.q: In northern Vietnam, nem rán are crispy fried what?
items.h: Northerners say nem rán and southerners say chả giò for the same crispy rolls.

items.q: What does the Vietnamese word 'ăn' mean?
items.h: Ăn means eat and uống means drink, so 'ăn uống' means eating and drinking.

items.q: Which is the longest river in Europe?
items.h: The Volga flows through Russia for about 3,500 km and into the Caspian Sea.

items.q: Mount Fuji is the highest mountain in which country?
items.h: Mount Fuji is a volcano with an almost perfect cone, often capped with snow.

items.q: The Great Barrier Reef lies off the coast of which country?
items.h: The Great Barrier Reef is built by billions of tiny coral animals.

items.q: Which desert in Chile is one of the driest places on Earth?
items.h: Parts of Chile's Atacama Desert get almost no rain for years at a time.

items.q: Which Italian city is built on over 100 islands linked by canals?
items.h: In Venice people get around by boat, along canals instead of streets.

items.q: What is the chemical symbol for silver?
items.h: Ag comes from argentum, Latin for silver; Argentina is named after silver too.

items.q: Which gas has the chemical formula CO2?
items.h: CO2 is one carbon atom joined to two oxygen atoms.

items.q: Who wrote three famous laws of motion in 1687?
items.h: Newton's first law: things stay still or keep moving unless a force acts on them.

items.q: Which unit measures how many times a second something vibrates?
items.h: Hertz counts vibrations per second; people hear from about 20 to 20,000 Hz.

items.q: Which metal is a liquid at room temperature?
items.h: Liquid mercury is so dense that a lump of iron floats on top of it.

items.q: Which space probe, launched in 1977, reached interstellar space?
items.h: Voyager 1 crossed into interstellar space in 2012, beyond the Sun's bubble of wind.

items.q: In 1957, Sputnik 1 became the first artificial what?
items.h: Sputnik 1 was a shiny metal ball that beeped radio signals as it circled Earth.

items.q: Which space object has gravity so strong that light cannot escape?
items.h: Black holes can't be seen directly, but scientists spot them by their pull on stars.

items.q: Which gas is the Sun mainly made of?
items.h: In the Sun's core, hydrogen fuses into helium and gives out light and heat.

items.q: Which space telescope, launched in 2021, sees in infrared light?
items.h: The James Webb Space Telescope has a gold-coated mirror 6.5 metres across.

items.q: What is the largest fish in the sea?
items.h: The whale shark is a gentle giant that eats tiny plankton; the blue whale is a mammal.

items.q: Which animal group do spiders and scorpions belong to?
items.h: Arachnids have eight legs and two body parts; insects have six legs and three parts.

items.q: What is the change from caterpillar to butterfly called?
items.h: Frogs and butterflies both go through metamorphosis, changing shape as they grow.

items.q: Which bird can hover and even fly backwards?
items.h: Hummingbirds beat their wings so fast that they hum.

items.q: Which of these animals is a crustacean?
items.h: Crustaceans, like crabs, lobsters and woodlice, have hard shells and jointed legs.

items.q: Which organ makes insulin and digestive juices?
items.h: The pancreas sits behind your stomach and sends digestive juices into your gut.

items.q: What carries messages between your brain and the rest of your body?
items.h: Signals along your fastest nerves travel at over 100 metres per second.

items.q: What is the proper name for your kneecap?
items.h: Your patella protects the front of your knee joint.

items.q: Which part of your body has fluid-filled tubes that sense balance?
items.h: Three looped tubes in your inner ear sense when your head turns or tilts.

items.q: What is it called when plants lose water through their leaves?
items.h: A big tree can give off hundreds of litres of water vapour on a hot day.

items.q: What are the stony spikes hanging from a cave's ceiling called?
items.h: Stalactites hold tight to the ceiling; stalagmites might grow up from the ground.

items.q: Which type of tall cloud brings thunderstorms?
items.h: Cumulonimbus clouds can tower over 10 km high and bring thunder and hail.

items.q: What is it called when water or wind wears rock away?
items.h: The Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon by erosion over millions of years.

items.q: Which Italian artist sketched flying machines over 500 years ago?
items.h: Leonardo da Vinci filled notebooks with ideas for flying machines and parachutes.

items.q: Which explorer charted Australia's east coast in 1770?
items.h: Captain Cook mapped Australia's east coast on his ship, the Endeavour.

items.q: Which German scientist discovered X-rays in 1895?
items.h: Wilhelm Röntgen received the very first Nobel Prize in Physics, in 1901.

items.q: Which ancient wonder was a giant bronze statue at a Greek harbour?
items.h: The Colossus of Rhodes was a bronze statue of Helios, the Greek sun god.

items.q: Which people carved the city of Petra into pink rock?
items.h: Petra, in Jordan, was carved into rose-pink sandstone cliffs over 2,000 years ago.

items.q: Which Dutch artist painted 'Girl with a Pearl Earring'?
items.h: Johannes Vermeer painted calm indoor scenes full of soft daylight.

items.q: Whose Ninth Symphony ends with the famous 'Ode to Joy'?
items.h: Beethoven wrote nine symphonies, and the Ode to Joy ends his last one.

items.q: Which Korean martial art is famous for its high kicks?
items.h: Taekwondo comes from Korea and has been an Olympic sport since 2000.

items.q: Which script is used to write Hindi?
items.h: Devanagari letters hang from a line drawn along the top of each word.

items.q: The piano's full Italian name, pianoforte, means what?
items.h: Early pianos amazed players because they could play both softly and loudly.

items.q: What do the five angles inside a pentagon add up to?
items.h: A pentagon can be split into 3 triangles: 3 × 180° = 540°.

items.q: Which of these is a square number?
items.h: 64 is a square number because 8 × 8 = 64.

items.q: What is the mean of 2, 4 and 9?
items.h: To find the mean, add the numbers up and divide by how many: 15 ÷ 3 = 5.

items.q: The giant caves of Phong Nha–Kẻ Bàng were carved out of which rock?
items.h: Rainwater slowly dissolves limestone, hollowing out caves over millions of years.

items.q: The Vietnamese letter đ, with a bar, sounds like which English letter?
items.h: Vietnamese đ sounds like English d, while a plain d sounds like z in the north.

items.q: Which part of the name Việt Nam means 'south'?
items.h: Nam means south, bắc means north, đông means east and tây means west.

items.q: Bánh cuốn are thin steamed sheets made from which grain?
items.h: Bánh cuốn sheets are steamed on a cloth, then rolled round pork and mushrooms.

items.q: Which Vietnamese sweet is made with beans, jelly or coconut milk?
items.h: Chè comes in dozens of kinds and can be served hot or with crushed ice.

items.q: Which Vietnamese zither has many strings and movable bridges?
items.h: The đàn tranh is plucked with finger picks; the đàn bầu has just one string.

items.q: Which fruit, thanh long in Vietnamese, has pink skin and green scales?
items.h: Dragon fruit grows on a climbing cactus; its flesh is white or red with tiny seeds.

items.q: What does the Vietnamese word 'bạn' mean?
items.h: Bạn means friend, and it is also a friendly way to say 'you'.

items.q: Which African river plunges over Victoria Falls?
items.h: Local people call Victoria Falls Mosi-oa-Tunya, 'the smoke that thunders'.

items.q: Which mountains in Russia are often used as Europe's eastern edge?
items.h: The Ural Mountains run from north to south, splitting Russia into Europe and Asia.

items.q: What is the capital of Argentina?
items.h: Buenos Aires means 'good airs' or 'fair winds' in Spanish.

items.q: Which is the largest island in the world?
items.h: Greenland is the largest island, because Australia counts as a continent.

items.q: Which sea is so salty that swimmers float on it easily?
items.h: The Dead Sea is almost ten times saltier than the ocean, so people float like corks.

items.q: What is the chemical symbol for potassium?
items.h: K comes from kalium, a Latin name for potassium; bananas are full of it.

items.q: Which is the lightest of all the elements?
items.h: Hydrogen is element number 1, the very first in the periodic table.

items.q: What is a material that lets heat pass through it easily called?
items.h: Metal pans conduct heat well, so their handles are often made of wood or plastic.

items.q: What is it called when a solid turns straight into a gas?
items.h: Dry ice, which is frozen carbon dioxide, turns straight into gas: it sublimes.

items.q: Sound travels fastest through which of these?
items.h: Sound moves about 17 times faster through steel than through air.

items.q: Mars looks red because its dust is full of what?
items.h: Iron oxide is rust, so the Red Planet's colour comes from rusty dust.

items.q: How many Earth days does Mercury take to orbit the Sun?
items.h: Mercury races round the Sun in 88 days; Venus takes 225 and Mars 687.

items.q: The main asteroid belt lies between Mars and which planet?
items.h: The biggest object in the asteroid belt, Ceres, is a dwarf planet.

items.q: Which mission first landed people on the Moon, in 1969?
items.h: Apollo 11's lunar module, the Eagle, landed in the Moon's Sea of Tranquillity.

items.q: Which shape best describes a planet's path around the Sun?
items.h: Johannes Kepler found that planets travel in ellipses, like slightly squashed circles.

items.q: Which big cat cannot fully pull in its claws?
items.h: A cheetah's claws stay out like a sprinter's spikes, gripping the ground as it runs.

items.q: Lizards bask in the sun because they are what?
items.h: Cold-blooded animals like lizards warm up in sunshine before they can be active.

items.q: Which bird flies from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back each year?
items.h: An Arctic tern sees two summers every year, one at each end of the world.

items.q: Which of these animals is a mollusc?
items.h: Molluscs, like snails, slugs, octopuses and clams, have soft bodies, often in a shell.

items.q: Which cells in your body fight germs?
items.h: White cells patrol your body and attack germs that get inside.

items.q: Which soft tissue inside your bones makes new red cells?
items.h: Your bone marrow makes millions of new red cells every second.

items.q: Which waste gas do your lungs get rid of when you breathe out?
items.h: Your cells make carbon dioxide as they release energy, and your lungs breathe it out.

items.q: Which dome-shaped muscle under your lungs helps you breathe?
items.h: When your diaphragm tightens and flattens, air rushes into your lungs.

items.q: Which part of your brain fine-tunes balance and movement?
items.h: The cerebellum, whose name means 'little brain', sits at the back of your head.

items.q: What is a scientist who studies rocks called?
items.h: Geologists read layers of rock like the pages of Earth's history book.

items.q: Which part of a flower makes pollen?
items.h: Stamens make pollen, and a flower's sticky stigma catches pollen from others.

items.q: What is the hardest natural mineral?
items.h: On the Mohs scale of hardness, diamond scores 10 and soft talc scores just 1.

items.q: Which instrument measures air pressure?
items.h: A falling barometer reading often means clouds and rain are on the way.

items.q: Which trees have needles and cones?
items.h: Most conifers, like pines and spruces, are evergreen and keep their needles all year.

items.q: Which people carved the giant moai statues on Easter Island?
items.h: The Rapa Nui people carved nearly 1,000 moai from volcanic rock.

items.q: Who argued in 1543 that Earth travels around the Sun?
items.h: Copernicus put the Sun, not Earth, at the centre of the planets' paths.

items.q: Which Egyptian city had a famous ancient library and lighthouse?
items.h: Alexandria's Pharos lighthouse was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

items.q: Who discovered Jupiter's four largest moons in 1610?
items.h: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto are still called the Galilean moons.

items.q: What did the Wright brothers fly at Kitty Hawk in 1903?
items.h: The Wright brothers' first powered flight lasted just 12 seconds.

items.q: Which country is flamenco dancing from?
items.h: Flamenco, from southern Spain, mixes guitar, singing, clapping and fast footwork.

items.q: Which of these languages is written from right to left?
items.h: Arabic and Hebrew are both written from right to left across the page.

items.q: Who wrote the play 'A Midsummer Night's Dream'?
items.h: Shakespeare wrote nearly 40 plays, many first shown at London's Globe Theatre.

items.q: Which Mexican artist painted self-portraits with flowers in her hair?
items.h: Frida Kahlo painted over 50 self-portraits, sometimes with her pet monkeys.

items.q: What is the lowest common multiple of 4 and 6?
items.h: Multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12… and of 6 are 6, 12… so 12 is the first they share.

items.q: How many centimetres are there in 2.5 metres?
items.h: There are 100 cm in a metre, so 2.5 m = 2.5 × 100 = 250 cm.

items.q: Which Roman numeral stands for 1,000?
items.h: In Roman numerals M stands for 1,000, D for 500 and C for 100.

items.q: What is 2 to the power of 5?
items.h: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32: start at 1 and double five times.

items.q: Hội An's old town was once a busy what?
items.h: From the 1500s, ships from Japan, China and Europe traded silk and spices at Hội An.

items.q: At Tết, what is 'xông đất'?
items.h: Families hope a cheerful, lucky person will be their first visitor of the new year.

items.q: How many animals are in the Vietnamese zodiac?
items.h: The 12 zodiac animals take turns, so each animal's year comes round every 12 years.

items.q: Which spicy lemongrass noodle soup comes from the old royal city?
items.h: Bún bò Huế is a spicy beef noodle soup flavoured with lemongrass and chilli.

items.q: In which part of Vietnam is the Hoàng Liên Sơn range?
items.h: The Hoàng Liên Sơn range in the northwest holds Fansipan, Vietnam's highest peak.

items.q: What is a sáo trúc?
items.h: Sáo means flute and trúc is a kind of bamboo, so a sáo trúc is a bamboo flute.

items.q: Cần Thơ, famous for its floating markets, lies in which delta?
items.h: Cần Thơ sits on a branch of the Mekong, and its floating markets start at dawn.

items.q: In Vietnamese, what does 'bà' usually mean?
items.h: Bà means grandmother and ông means grandfather.

items.q: Which canal lets ships cross from the Atlantic to the Pacific?
items.h: The Panama Canal cuts across Central America, saving ships a trip round South America.

items.q: Which country is famous for its deep, steep-sided fjords?
items.h: Fjords are long, deep sea inlets carved out by glaciers between steep cliffs.

items.q: What is a piece of land almost surrounded by water called?
items.h: Italy, Korea and Florida are all peninsulas, joined to land on just one side.

items.q: When it is summer in Britain, which season is it in Australia?
items.h: The hemispheres take turns tilting towards the Sun, so their seasons are opposite.

items.q: In which country is Angel Falls, the highest waterfall on Earth?
items.h: Angel Falls drops nearly 1 km, mostly in one long, unbroken plunge.

items.q: What is the chemical symbol for lead?
items.h: Pb comes from plumbum, Latin for lead, which also gives us the word plumber.

items.q: What are the rows across the periodic table called?
items.h: Elements in the same period have the same number of electron shells.

items.q: Roughly how fast does light travel?
items.h: Light could zip round the Earth about seven and a half times in one second.

items.q: In a parallel circuit, if one bulb breaks, the others do what?
items.h: Each bulb in a parallel circuit has its own loop, which is how homes are wired.

items.q: What is the pH of pure water?
items.h: On the pH scale, 7 is neutral; acids are below 7 and alkalis are above.

items.q: Which of these is an acid?
items.h: Lemon juice and vinegar are acids; soap and baking soda are alkalis.

items.q: What are Saturn's rings mostly made of?
items.h: Saturn's rings are countless chunks of ice, some as tiny as dust, some as big as houses.

items.q: Which planet was found in 1846 after maths predicted where it was?
items.h: Uranus wobbled in its orbit, so astronomers worked out where Neptune must be.

items.q: What is the Sun's outer atmosphere, seen in a total eclipse, called?
items.h: The Sun's corona glows like a pearly halo when the Moon covers the Sun.

items.q: When the Moon is waxing, what is its lit part doing?
items.h: A waxing Moon looks bigger each night; a waning Moon looks smaller.

items.q: What is a group of owls called?
items.h: A group of owls is a parliament, and a group of flamingos is a flamboyance.

items.q: What is a baby whale called?
items.h: A blue whale calf drinks hundreds of litres of its mother's milk every day.

items.q: Which animal carries its baby for about 22 months before it is born?
items.h: An elephant calf can stand up within an hour or so of being born.

items.q: What is a honeybee's 'waggle dance' for?
items.h: The waggle dance tells other bees which way to fly to find flowers, and how far.

items.q: Which salamander, the 'Mexican walking fish', keeps its gills?
items.h: The axolotl is an amphibian that keeps its frilly gills all its life.

items.q: Which vitamin are oranges, kiwis and peppers full of?
items.h: Your body cannot store much vitamin C, so it needs some fruit and vegetables every day.

items.q: Where in your body does digestion begin?
items.h: Saliva starts breaking down starch as soon as you start chewing.

items.q: Under the enamel, what is most of a tooth made of?
items.h: Under the hard enamel a tooth is mostly dentine, with soft pulp in the middle.

items.q: Your heart and its vessels make up which body system?
items.h: Laid end to end, your body's vessels would stretch more than twice round the Earth.

items.q: What is a plant that lives for many years called?
items.h: Annuals live for one year, but perennials like trees keep growing year after year.

items.q: Which gas high in the sky absorbs much of the Sun's UV light?
items.h: The ozone layer in the stratosphere works like sunscreen for the whole planet.

items.q: Where a wide river meets the sea, what is the area called?
items.h: An estuary mixes river and sea water, making a rich home for birds and fish.

items.q: In which type of rock are most fossils found?
items.h: Fossils form in layers of mud and sand, which slowly harden into sedimentary rock.

items.q: What is a hot spring that shoots water and steam into the air?
items.h: Old Faithful in Yellowstone is a famous geyser that spouts many times a day.

items.q: Which British scientist discovered the electron in 1897?
items.h: J. J. Thomson found the electron, the first known particle smaller than an atom.

items.q: Who showed in 1831 that moving magnets can make electricity?
items.h: Michael Faraday's discovery is how power stations make electricity with spinning magnets.

items.q: Which ancient people built the step pyramid at Chichén Itzá?
items.h: Chichén Itzá's pyramid, El Castillo, has 365 steps, one for each day of the year.

items.q: Louis Braille invented a way of reading by touching what?
items.h: Louis Braille was only 15 when he invented his raised-dot alphabet.

items.q: At which festival in Spain do crowds throw tomatoes?
items.h: La Tomatina takes place each August in the small town of Buñol, near Valencia.

items.q: Where were the first modern Olympic Games held, in 1896?
items.h: The 1896 Games in Athens brought back the ancient Greek Olympics in a new form.

items.q: 'Guten Tag' means 'good day' in which language?
items.h: German is spoken in Germany, Austria and parts of Switzerland.

items.q: Which composer wrote the music for the ballet 'The Nutcracker'?
items.h: Tchaikovsky also wrote the music for the ballets Swan Lake and Sleeping Beauty.

items.q: What is the art of beautiful handwriting called?
items.h: At Tết in Vietnam, calligraphers write lucky words on red paper for families.

items.q: How many sides does a nonagon have?
items.h: A heptagon has 7 sides, an octagon 8, a nonagon 9 and a decagon 10.

items.q: What is 0.25 as a fraction?
items.h: 0.25 means 25 hundredths, and 25/100 simplifies to 1/4.

items.q: What is the volume of a cube with 3 cm sides?
items.h: Volume of a cube = side × side × side, so 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cubic centimetres.

items.q: Which number is a factor of 36 but not of 24?
items.h: The factors of 36 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18 and 36.

items.q: Which famous ancient bronze drums come from early Vietnam?
items.h: Đông Sơn drums, over 2,000 years old, are decorated with birds, boats and dancers.

items.q: Which mountain pass between Huế and Đà Nẵng is famous for sea views?
items.h: Hải Vân means 'sea clouds': the pass is often wrapped in mist above the sea.

items.q: What does 'bánh' mean in names like bánh mì and bánh chưng?
items.h: Bánh covers all sorts of cakes, breads and dumplings, sweet or savoury.

items.q: Which monkey with a golden face lives on Đà Nẵng's Sơn Trà peninsula?
items.h: Red-shanked doucs have grey bodies, red 'socks', white arms and golden faces.

items.q: The Marble Mountains, five rocky hills, stand near which city?
items.h: The five Marble Mountains are named after five elements: metal, wood, water, fire, earth.

items.q: Ba Bể, in Vietnam's northern mountains, is a famous natural what?
items.h: Ba Bể is Vietnam's largest natural lake, ringed by limestone mountains and forest.

items.q: What does the Vietnamese word 'nhà' mean?
items.h: Nhà means house or home, so 'về nhà' means 'go home'.

items.q: Roughly how long is Vietnam from its northern tip to its southern tip?
items.h: Vietnam is long and thin: about 1,650 km long but only about 50 km wide at its narrowest.

items.q: What is the capital of New Zealand?
items.h: Wellington, at the southern tip of the North Island, is New Zealand's capital.

items.q: Ancient Mesopotamia lay between the Tigris and which river?
items.h: Mesopotamia means 'land between rivers' in Greek.

items.q: North of which line can the Sun shine at midnight in summer?
items.h: North of the Arctic Circle the Sun stays up all night around midsummer: the midnight sun.

items.q: Vientiane is the capital of which country?
items.h: Vientiane sits on the banks of the Mekong, across the river from Thailand.

items.q: What are Africa's wide, warm grasslands with scattered trees called?
items.h: The African savannah is home to lions, zebras, giraffes and elephants.

items.q: What is the chemical symbol for copper?
items.h: Cu comes from cuprum, the Latin word for copper, named after the island of Cyprus.

items.q: Which Russian chemist published his famous periodic table in 1869?
items.h: Dmitri Mendeleev left gaps in his table for elements that had not been found yet.

items.q: Which unit is used to measure electrical power?
items.h: The watt is named after James Watt, the Scottish steam-engine engineer.

items.q: Which simple machine is a sloping surface, like a ramp?
items.h: A longer, gentler ramp needs less push to raise a heavy load.

items.q: When salt dissolves completely in water, what do you get?
items.h: In a solution the salt is still there: boil the water away and the salt is left behind.

items.q: Which planet takes about 165 Earth years to orbit the Sun?
items.h: Neptune was found in 1846 and finished its first orbit since then in 2011.

items.q: Pluto orbits in which icy region beyond Neptune?
items.h: The Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune is full of icy worlds, including Pluto.

items.q: Who was the first person to float outside a spacecraft, in 1965?
items.h: Alexei Leonov's first spacewalk lasted about 12 minutes.

items.q: A nebula, where stars are born, is a huge cloud of what?
items.h: Inside a nebula, gravity pulls gas and dust together until new stars light up.

items.q: Which sea animal can grow back a lost arm?
items.h: Starfish, also called sea stars, can regrow lost arms over many months.

items.q: Which group of animals do penguins belong to?
items.h: Penguins are birds that cannot fly, but their wings make superb flippers.

items.q: What is an animal that is hunted and eaten by others called?
items.h: In a food chain a rabbit is prey for a fox, and the fox is a predator.

items.q: Which animal makes its home in a holt?
items.h: Otters live in holts, badgers in setts, rabbits in warrens and foxes in dens.

items.q: Your brain, spinal cord and nerves make up which system?
items.h: Your brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system, the body's control centre.

items.q: Which forearm bone is on the same side as your thumb?
items.h: Your forearm has two bones: the radius on the thumb side and the ulna on the other.

items.q: Which part of your eye controls how much light gets in?
items.h: In dim light your iris opens the pupil wide; in bright light it makes it small.

items.q: How many ribs do most people have altogether?
items.h: Most people have 24 ribs, in 12 pairs, which protect the heart and lungs.

items.q: Which part of vegetables and wholegrains keeps your gut moving?
items.h: Fibre from fruit, vegetables, beans and wholegrain bread helps food move through you.

items.q: What is the place where a river begins called?
items.h: A river's source is often a spring, a lake or melting snow high in the hills.

items.q: What is it called when animals make a long journey each year?
items.h: Swallows that nest in Britain migrate thousands of kilometres to Africa for the winter.

items.q: In which part of a plant cell does photosynthesis happen?
items.h: Chloroplasts are tiny green parts of plant cells, packed with chlorophyll.

items.q: What is a cold, treeless land with frozen ground underneath called?
items.h: Under the tundra lies permafrost, ground that stays frozen all year round.

items.q: Which Greek's famous theorem is about right-angled triangles?
items.h: Pythagoras' theorem says that in a right-angled triangle, a² + b² = c².

items.q: Which Chinese admiral led huge treasure fleets in the 1400s?
items.h: Zheng He's treasure ships sailed as far as East Africa over 600 years ago.

items.q: Who built the first electric battery, in 1800?
items.h: The volt, the unit of electrical push, is named after Alessandro Volta.

items.q: What was the Silk Road?
items.h: The Silk Road carried silk, spices and ideas between China and Europe.

items.q: Which Scottish engineer greatly improved the steam engine?
items.h: Watt's engines used far less coal and helped to power the first big factories.

items.q: The sitar is a stringed instrument from which country?
items.h: A sitar can have around 20 strings, and many of them hum along in sympathy.

items.q: What is the Korean alphabet called?
items.h: King Sejong created Hangul in the 1440s so that everyone could learn to read.

items.q: Which Dutch artist painted 'The Night Watch'?
items.h: Rembrandt's The Night Watch is a huge painting in Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum.

items.q: Which Italian city is famous for its leaning bell tower?
items.h: The Leaning Tower of Pisa began to tilt in the 1170s, while it was still being built.

items.q: How many players from each team are on a basketball court?
items.h: James Naismith invented basketball in 1891, with peach baskets for hoops.

items.q: What comes next: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, …?
items.h: In the Fibonacci sequence each number is the sum of the two before it: 5 + 8 = 13.

items.q: What is pi to two decimal places?
items.h: Pi is any circle's circumference divided by its diameter.

items.q: How big is each angle in an equilateral triangle?
items.h: The three equal angles share 180°, so each one is 180 ÷ 3 = 60°.

items.q: What is the perimeter of a square with 7 cm sides?
items.h: A square has four equal sides, so its perimeter is 4 × 7 = 28 cm.

items.q: What is a whole number above 1 that is not prime called?
items.h: Composite numbers, like 4, 9 and 15, have more than two factors.
